The photograph and report preserve an early Saugus athlete’s sporting life beyond high school. His Saugus playing and graduation years are estimated by the contributor at approximately 1905–1906; the clipping does not establish those dates. Source: Boston Globe, 1911.

photos.title: The 1928 football team
photos.caption: Fred Beresford’s 1928 team brought a new generation onto Stackpole’s Field. The yearbook recalls forty-five candidates but only two returning varsity men, captain Reggie Goss and Gilman Cann, and describes a squad whose oldest player was seventeen. Carroll Freeman, Red Hunnewell, Stuart Kidder and Jim Foley emerge as central figures in its account of hard work and determined play. Kidder, a first-year player who became the leading ground-gainer, provided a memorable Thanksgiving highlight with a pass to Goss that gained more than sixty yards. Saugus lost that muddy finale to Mission High of Roxbury, 6–0, but the yearbook honored the seniors’ effort and the resolve of a team that kept fighting against heavier opposition. The original portrait and two newly added review pages preserve the players, their positions, the Thanksgiving game and the hopes placed in the next generation. The seven wins in eleven games mentioned in the opening historical passage belong to 1927, not the 1928 season.
photos.dateSource: 1928 is written on the photograph; correction confirmed by Sal Nicolo, October 2026.

images.title: 1928 season review · a young team under Fred Beresford
images.caption: The yearbook traces the senior class’s football experience from 1925 through 1928. After a 1927 team coached by Benny Rice won seven of eleven games, Fred Beresford returned for 1928. Forty-five candidates answered the call, but Reggie Goss and Gilman Cann were the only returning varsity men identified at the outset. Goss was elected captain. The account describes an unusually young squad: its oldest player was seventeen, most were sixteen, and speedy Larry Templeman was only fifteen. Carroll Freeman earned a place at left tackle, Red Hunnewell played guard, and newcomer Stuart Kidder won the fullback position and led the team in yardage.
images.dateSource: Yearbook scan supplied and season identified by Sal Nicolo; publication-year differences noted in the caption.

images.title: 1928 Thanksgiving · a determined stand in the mud
images.caption: On Thanksgiving morning at Stackpole’s Field, Saugus faced the heavier Mission High team from Roxbury on a surface covered by three or four inches of mud. Mission won 6–0, but the yearbook praised Saugus’s effort before the season’s largest home crowd. Stuart Kidder’s pass to Reggie Goss produced a gain of more than sixty yards. Freeman, Hunnewell and Goss anchored a stubborn left side, while Kidder, Kelley and Jim Foley earned praise in the backfield. Foley, who played with one arm, was singled out for his tackling, passing and spirit. The page also records the first-string lineup and looks ahead to captain-elect Ernie Castle and returning players Lawrence Templeman, Jimmy Glinski, Mike Gifford and Bill MacKay.
images.dateSource: Yearbook scan supplied and season identified by Sal Nicolo; publication-year differences noted in the caption.

photos.title: The 1929 football team
photos.caption: Coach Rice’s 1929 Sachems began with consecutive shutout victories over Manchester and Swampscott. The 12–0 Swampscott result was especially significant: the yearbook described it as Saugus’s first victory over that rival. Templeman supplied the finishing runs, while Roveto’s passing and the receiving of Gates and Quint helped move the offense. Injuries and a demanding schedule tested the team, including captain Quint’s knee injury against Milton and tackle Ed Newbury’s broken wrist at Chelsea. A 27–6 victory over Rockport showcased Templeman’s big-play running, with touchdown runs of 70, 44 and 35 yards. The squad portrait and companion game account, published in the 1930 Tontoquonian, offer a detailed view of the preceding fall’s players and performances. The supplied results page ends with Chelsea and does not document the complete season record.

images.title: 1929 season · game-by-game yearbook account
images.caption: Published in the 1930 Tontoquonian, this page reviews the preceding fall. Saugus opened September 28 at Stackpole’s Field with a 22–0 victory over Manchester: Templeman scored twice, Gifford once, and Gates added a safety. A 12–0 victory over Swampscott followed, described by the yearbook as Saugus’s first football win over that opponent. Roveto’s passing to Gates and Quint helped set up one Templeman touchdown; Templeman later added a 25-yard scoring run. Losses followed against Milton (15–0), Essex Aggies (15–0) and Reading (12–0). Saugus rebounded against Rockport, 27–6, with Templeman scoring on runs of 70, 44 and 35 yards and Muzzey adding another touchdown. Chelsea won the next recorded game, 24–6, with Templeman scoring for Saugus. Captain Quint injured his right knee against Milton, while tackle Ed Newbury broke his right wrist against Chelsea. This page does not include the Danvers result or establish the complete season record.

photos.title: The 1930 football team
photos.caption: Led by captain Jim Muzzy and Coach Rice, the 1930 Sachems were celebrated in their yearbook as Saugus’s best football team since the undefeated 1922 squad. A 30–0 opening victory over Manchester set the tone, while Laurie Templeman’s speed and scoring and Muzzy’s passing, tackling and steady leadership gave the backfield its character. Rice’s tribute also recognized Jimmie Glinski, Albie Day, Harry Raddin, Eddie Newbury, Stewart Quint, Foster and Gordon Baker, emphasizing the line play, blocking and persistence behind the team’s success. The squad photograph commemorates a 14–0 victory over Danvers with a handwritten 1930 notation. Its printed “Football Squad of 1931” caption reflects a dating difference retained in the image and explained here; the gallery follows the 1930 season identification supplied by Sal Nicolo. Beyond the games, the review honors the cheerleaders and recalls a Parent Teachers’ Association banquet at which nine seniors received sweaters and returning players received letters. Together, the portrait and written tribute preserve a season remembered for strong play, shared effort and community pride. The supplied page does not establish an exact final season record.

images.title: 1930 season · Captain Jim Muzzy & Coach Rice’s tribute
images.caption: The yearbook called this Saugus’s best team since the unbeaten 1922 eleven. Coach Rice’s squad opened with a 30–0 win over Manchester and was led by captain Jim Muzzy, whose surname appears elsewhere as Muzzey. Rice praised Jimmie Glinski’s strength in the line, Albie Day at center, Harry Raddin at offensive end, Eddie Newbury’s determination despite an injured wrist, and Stewart Quint’s steady improvement at tackle. Foster was credited with directing the offense, Gordon Baker with effective blocking, and Laurie Templeman with speed and scoring ability. Muzzy earned praise as a consistent all-around contributor, blocker, tackler and passer, and as a scoring threat second only to Templeman. Frances Keough directed the cheerleaders, supported by Eunice Shea, Florence Russell, Elwin Shaw and Charles Brostrom. At the Parent Teachers’ Association football banquet, nine seniors received sweaters and younger squad members received letters. Captain Muzzy and Coach Rice spoke, while musical entertainment and impersonations completed the celebration. The account does not supply a full won–lost record.

photos.title: The 1939 Sachems · a season to remember
photos.caption: The 1939 North Shore champions. The 1939 Sachems gave Saugus a season to remember. Under head coach Charles “Buzz” Harvey and assistant Nick Morris, a team that began amid modest expectations answered a 12–0 opening defeat at Medford with ten unbeaten games, finishing 9–1–1. Co-captains Jimmy Duffy and Stan Green helped lead a squad whose resilience, teamwork and determined play earned growing recognition across the region. Mike Harrington, Eddie Shipulski, Fred Walkey, Ray Mansfield, Dexter Pratt, Joe Bucherie, Woody Dill and Del Pitman figure prominently in the yearbook’s accounts, while the named squad portrait preserves Art Statuto and the teammates whose contributions made the season possible. Shutout victories over Gloucester, Swampscott and Marblehead built momentum, but the defining afternoon came against Salem. Before a crowd the yearbook estimated at 10,000, Saugus prevailed 3–0 on Bucherie’s field goal, with Harrington holding, backed by a defense that kept the Witches scoreless. A 38–6 Thanksgiving victory over Danvers provided a fitting farewell for the seniors. The celebration reached beyond the field: supporters traveled to Gloucester by special train, the squad enjoyed a Christmas holiday trip to New York and West Point, and 1,000 fans attended the January 20 banquet at the Lynn Armory. These seven yearbook pages preserve more than scores. Together, the action photographs, roster, co-captain portraits and celebrations honor a team that turned an uncertain beginning into an enduring source of Sachem pride—and the community that stood behind it.

photos.title: Saugus Preps for Chelsea · Buzz Harvey’s 1940 outlook
photos.caption:
Boston Globe reporter Herbert Ralby previews Saugus’s 1940 opener against Chelsea under the lights at Chelsea Memorial Stadium. Charlie “Buzz” Harvey, beginning his fourth season as head coach, had a 40-player squad, his largest at Saugus. He looked to build on the previous year’s nine wins and one tie in 11 games, with Medford responsible for the only defeat.

Co-captains Mike Harrington and George Flaherty led the returning talent. Harvey praised Harrington and Eddie Shipulski as junior backs who could kick, pass and run. Tommy Atkins returned at quarterback, while Bob Porter, Ed Koska and Phil Hand competed for the fullback spot. The projected line included Ken Parker at center, George and Len Flaherty at guard, Ed and Stan Wladkowski at end, and Joe MacDonald and Bob Connell at tackle. The article contrasts Saugus’s optimism with the rebuilding task facing first-year Chelsea coach Henry McCarthy.

photos.caption: One of the defining teams of the Sachems’ golden era, John Janusas’s 1949 squad finished 10–1 and won the Exchange Bowl. Co-captains Sardi Nicolo and Dan Murphy led a team featuring Richie Nicolo and Fred Quinlan. The report emphasizes Richie Nicolo’s importance to the offense and his expected return after missing the opener through suspension. It also highlights Saugus’s depth, with capable substitutes and promising younger players competing for places. Mack places the outlook in the context of the program’s rapid rise, recalling the previous season’s postseason victory over Weymouth at Manning Bowl and a campaign with only one defeat. Janusas’s confidence was tempered by criticism of the team’s opening performance and a demand for improvement in practice. The full sports page is preserved here, with the Saugus column running down the left side.

photos.title: Only two veterans return · Janusas rebuilds Saugus in 1951
photos.caption:
The Boston Globe’s “Schoolboy Sidelights” column examines Saugus’s uncertain outlook after a highly regarded 1950 season. Coach John Janusas had only two returning veterans: guard Charlie Murphy and Tony Serino, a fullback converted to quarterback during fall practice.

Janusas had hoped in the spring that he had found a replacement for Richie Nicolo, but that candidate enlisted in the Army. Serino, listed at 5 feet 9 inches and about 155 pounds, was therefore moved to quarterback. The article praises his passing and knowledge of the plays while noting that he was learning a new position. It describes a sizable line and enough replacements in both numbers and size. With Revere and Cambridge Latin scheduled for the first two games, Janusas hoped the inexperienced squad would develop enough to produce some surprises. photos.title: Saugus rallies past Revere, 24–6 · September 15, 1951

Norman Taylor recovered a Revere fumble to set up the tying score, and quarterback Tony Serino then connected with Bob Meagher on a 58-yard touchdown play for a 12–6 lead.

The Sachems added two dramatic scores: a 62-yard return after a defender took a Revere handoff in the backfield, and a 32-yard blocked-punt return by guard Charlie Murphy. The report states that Revere had not beaten Saugus since 1920. The clipping also preserves the teams’ lineups and scoring by quarter.

photos.title: The 1953 North Shore champions · team & season review
photos.caption: The 1953 Sachems earned their place in Saugus football history as North Shore champions, led by co-captains John Leahy and Doug MacNeill under coach John Janusas. These seven yearbook pages bring together the full squad and named roster, player portraits set against newspaper headlines, detailed game accounts and three collections of photographs from the field and stands. The season demanded both resilience and teamwork. Saugus opened with shutouts of Revere and Lynn Classical, rallied for a 12–12 tie with Marblehead, and edged Beverly 14–13 in a game the yearbook remembered as a thriller. A 26–18 victory over Lynn English kept the Sachems moving forward before Chelsea delivered their only regular-season defeat. They answered with a 27–0 win over Salem, then finished decisively on Thanksgiving, defeating Peabody 33–6 to secure the North Shore League title. Billy MacNeill, Bill Whittredge, Bob Piwowarski, Mal Rice and Charlie and Jackie Lawrence feature throughout the accounts, alongside the linemen and teammates who made the scoring drives and defensive stops possible. The yearbook records a 6–1–1 season and lists the 18–6 Joyce Jamboree loss to Haverhill separately. Together, these pages honor the players, coaches, managers, band and supporters who shared in a memorable championship autumn.
photos.dateSource: Contributed yearbook pages explicitly describe the 1953 North Shore championship season.

photos.title: The 1954 Sachems · squad, co-captains & season review
photos.caption: The 1954 Sachems finished 6–3 under head coach John Janusas, with co-captains Jack Lawrence and Malcolm “Mal” Rice leading a squad whose season combined strong running, determined line play and a winning Thanksgiving finish. Saugus opened by shutting out Revere, 20–0, and went on to beat Marblehead, Chelsea, Amesbury and Winthrop before closing with a 20–12 victory at Peabody. The nine printed results total 171 points for Saugus and 98 for its opponents. Rice and Bob Piwowarski feature prominently in the running accounts, while Charlie Lawrence’s passing, Fred Case’s long runs and Paul Downing’s receiving and timely fumble recovery appear throughout the review. The yearbook also celebrates the work of Billy Ellis, Bob Lancaster, Tommy Mullen, Ed Olley, Fred Bradley, Ted Dwyer, Ken Ballard and Fred MacDonald in the line. A 77-yard run by Case against Lynn English, Rice’s 71-yard score against Chelsea, and Fred Orlando’s 92-yard touchdown against Winthrop preserve some of the season’s most memorable individual plays. These six pages bring together the full schedule, a named team portrait, co-captain portraits, individual player studies and action photographs from the jamboree and regular season. They also preserve the community around the team and a Thanksgiving farewell to the graduating players. photos.title: Saugus romps, two Serino TDs · 40–0 over Lynn English
photos.caption: Chris Serino scored twice as first-place Saugus defeated Lynn English, 40–0. Chuck Shipulski’s interception return to the English 9 set up Serino’s first touchdown; his second came on a 24-yard run after a lateral from Jim Paolini. The Boston Globe report places the unbeaten Sachems at 5–0 and atop the North Shore League at that point in the season. Source: Boston Globe, 1966.

photos.title: Saugus, Once Doormat, Now Class A Contender · 1966
photos.caption: Neil Singelais’s October 3, 1966 Boston Globe feature charts Saugus’s resurgence under Walter Sheridan after opening wins over Boston College High, 33–6, and Beverly, 36–8. The veteran backfield of Chris Serino, Jim Paolini, Mike Kimball and Ed McGuire anchors the story. Sheridan credits a balanced offense and a quick line, highlighting tackle John Dancewicz and center John Hanson. The article captures the excitement of a 2–0 start and renewed Class A hopes. Source: Boston Globe, October 3, 1966.

photos.title: Saugus whips Beverly, 36–8 · October 1966
photos.caption: Chris Serino’s long passes and Jim Paolini’s finishing runs powered Saugus to a 36–8 North Shore League victory over Beverly. Paolini scored three touchdowns, while a fourth-quarter recovery of a Beverly fumble helped set up another score. Beverly’s touchdown came on Glen Randall’s 85-yard kickoff return. The October 2, 1966 Boston Sunday Globe report records Saugus’s second straight win. Source: Boston Globe.

photos.title: The 1969 Sachems · squad & season photographs
photos.caption: The 1969 Sachems finished 7–2 under Paul Maguire, led by captains John Richard, Richard Conti and William Babcock. These three yearbook pages preserve the squad portrait and named roster, season review, regional honors, complete results, and photographs of the players and coaches. Victories included a 3–0 shutout of Woburn and a narrow 28–26 win over Newburyport. The team’s only defeats came against Class B champion Swampscott and Class A champion Peabody. Bob Osgood and Bill Eichel earned first offensive-team Northeastern Conference All-Star honors, Steve Nelson made the first defensive team, and Rich Desisto, Bill Babcock, Rich Conti and John Richard received honorable mentions. The yearbook celebrates a successful season without explicitly awarding Saugus a conference championship.
